items.title: Meet Yostin Peña, the man of the hour in the Yankees’ system
items.author: Andrés Chávez
items.content:
The Yankees have plenty of talent in their minor league affiliates, so much so that young outfielder Yostin Peña, arguably the hottest hitter in the entire organization, isn’t yet ranked in MLB Pipeline’s top 30 prospects.

Peña, signed last December after issues regarding his age documentation surfaced and scuttled his deal with the St. Louis Cardinals, made quick work of the Dominican Summer League, slashing a robust .375/.457/.646 with eight homers, 27 stolen bases, and a 150 wRC+ in 37 games, before earning a promotion to Single-A.

There, the 18-year-old phenom has posted a brilliant .355/.419/.605 line with five round-trippers, seven thefts, and a 161 wRC+ in 18 games through Tuesday. Between the two levels, the dynamic talent has 13 dingers, 34 steals, and a 154 wRC+.

Peña has some of the most exciting raw tools you will see in the low minors, and an incredible frame for such a young prospect: he is 6’4” and is listed at 205 lb. Evidently, speed and athleticism are both plus, as is his raw power.

What has the industry said about him recently? In a fantasy baseball roundup, the folks at Baseball America said that Peña is ‘the highest-ranked hitting prospect still in Low-A. With excellent power for his age, a better-than-average in-zone contact rate and 15-to-20 stolen base potential, Peña is a fascinating blend of power, speed and fantasy upside.’

That’s nice for our fantasy baseball community, but what about as a real-life report? Sam Dyksra and Jonathan Mayo of MLB Pipeline recently reviewed the hottest hitter in each team’s farm system, and of course Peña’s name came up when they discussed the Yankees. Here’s what they wrote on August 26:

At 18 years old, Pena was a bit on the older side for the Dominican Summer League, where he opened the season, but on July 28, he skipped the FCL to get a promotion to Single-A Tampa and hasn’t looked back since. The 6-foot-4 right-handed slugger has hit .358/.389/.597 with four homers in his first 15 games with the Tarpons. (Three of those four dingers have come in the last week alone.) His big-time power (113.6 mph max exit velocity, 108.2 90th-percentile EV in the FSL) is his most intriguing asset, though a high chase rate brings some cause for concern as he sees more full-season pitching.

As you can see, those are some impressive exit velocities. Considering that he can still fill out his frame with muscle and thump, his raw power potential is very scary. It’s important to remember that he is still very young and raw, and given his contact issues and propensity to chase pitches out of the zone, he probably won’t be a fast riser who will get to Triple-A in the first half of 2027.

Speaking of his high chase rate, Peña’s 39.7 O-Swing% is quite high. Additionally, he has a 16.1 SwStr%, also elevated. Both marks would rank near the bottom of the league in the majors, and this is against Single-A pitching. Stats don’t actually mean much since it’s just 18 games, but it’s something to keep an eye on. Amazingly, his 17.4 percent strikeout rate in those 18 Single-A games is not that bad, but that look under the hood suggests it could be much worse.

Despite his less-than-ideal approach and contact profile, Peña is an exciting prospect, indeed. Those who have seen him play believe he has superstar potential, but he needs to conquer some demons first. It’s nothing uncommon when talking about a prospect his age, though. The range of outcomes is broad here, but if Peña hits his lofty ceiling, watch out.

items.title: Back from injury, RailRiders reliever MacGregor making up for lost time
items.author: Scott Walsh
items.content:
Travis MacGregor came within one pitch of an immaculate inning in the top of the first Aug. 23 at PNC Field in northeastern Pennsylvania against the Charlotte Knights, Triple-A affiliate of the Chicago White Sox.

Forced to make a spot start for the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders, the 28-year-old right-hander struck out Rikuu Nishida on three pitches leading off the game. Then, he fanned Junior Perez on three pitches. He threw two strikes to Edgar Quero before Quero spoiled the bid by flying out to center field.

It was part of a perfect three-inning performance with four strikeouts and helped send the RailRiders on their way to a 9-5 victory.

MacGregor is pitching after starting the season on the 60-day injured list due to a shoulder injury suffered early in spring training. Since being activated Aug. 13, he has appeared in five games for the RailRiders. He allowed a run in his first game Aug. 13 at Lehigh Valley, but has not given up a run in the other four outings. He has 13 strikeouts in 9.2 innings.

Signed by the Yankees to a minor-league contract in December as a free agent, the injury prevented MacGregor from showing his new team what he can do. He is trying to make up for lost time.

“Any time you come to a new organization, you want to be able to showcase what you’re able to do,” MacGregor said. “Having to sit out for this long a time certainly was a little frustrating. But I’ve got a month left in the season pretty much to try to showcase my abilities. We’ll see what happens for the rest of the year.”

At the same time, he has to be careful not to do too much lest he reinjure himself.

“When I say showcase my abilities, I mean going out there and playing the way I play,” he said. “They liked something. They brought me in for a reason. I just have to go out there and play my game and showcase me for the amount of time I have. You can’t put too much pressure on yourself to try to make anything happen. That’s out of your control. I just have to make sure I’m prepared for each game that comes.”

This is MacGregor’s ninth minor-league season and he has a career record of 20-37 with eight saves and a 4.62 ERA in 238 games with 552 strikeouts in 541.2 innings. He was selected out of high school by the Pittsburgh Pirates in the second round (68th overall) of the 2016 MLB Draft. He was with the Pirates organization from 2016-18 and 2021-23, missing all of the 2019 season due to Tommy John surgery and the 2020 campaign due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

He signed with the Los Angeles Angels as a free agent for 2024 and spent one season in their system. In 2025, he signed as a free agent with the Texas Rangers and pitched at Double-A before being released at the end of July. He was picked up by the Milwaukee Brewers in August and finished the season in Double-A. He again became a free agent and was signed by the Yankees.

“It’s been a fantastic experience,” MacGregor said. “I’ve really enjoyed getting to know all the players and staff members, the coaches. Everyone’s been great. It’s the New York Yankees. They’re talked of highly and certainly met the standards they set for themselves. I’ve really enjoyed my time here so far.”

Unfortunately, his time with the Yankees got off to a rough start due to the injury in spring training. Beginning at the end of July, he made three rehab appearances with the Single-A Tampa Tarpons and one with the High-A Hudson Valley Renegades before joining the RailRiders.

“Anytime anybody comes off an injury, you’re wanting to try it out or feel it out for the first couple of pitches or outings,” MacGregor said. “But you’ve done so much preparation beforehand that you have to have confidence that you’re good to go. I’ve been throwing bullpens, throwing lives, stuff like that beforehand. I knew I was in good shape.”

This is not MacGregor’s first time in Triple-A. He made it to the highest level of the minors with the Pirates organization, as well as with the Angels. He has yet to make that next step to the major leagues, however.

“I wouldn’t say anything preventing me. Maybe just some unfortunate timing on things,” MacGregor said. “I’m just grateful to be playing any chance that I get. I’m confident my day will come. Until then, I’ll just be where my feet are and take care of business every day.”

Alexander Cornielle became the latest member of the RailRiders to earn an International League weekly award when the righthander was named Pitcher of the Week for the period of Aug. 24-30. He was honored for his shutout performance Aug. 28 at Worcester, going eight innings — a season-high for a RailRiders pitcher — and allowing just two hits with two walks and six strikeouts in a 2-0 win. It was the team’s ninth shutout of the season.

Since coming off the 60-day injured list and joining the RailRiders in June, Cornielle is 5-3 in 14 games (13 starts) with a 2.70 earned-run average and 59 strikeouts in 60 innings. However, in August, he was 2-1 in five starts with a 1.50 ERA and 25 strikeouts in 24 innings.

Cornielle joins Brendan Beck as RailRiders to be named IL Pitcher of the Week this season; Beck won the award three times (May 11-17, June 1-8, July 20-26) and also was chosen IL Pitcher of the Month for June. Yanquiel Fernandez (May 18-24) and Tyler Hardman (July 6-12) were selected IL Player of the Week this season.

items.title: Clarke Schmidt is getting ready to give Yankees’ bullpen a boost
items.author: Andrés Chávez
items.content:
The Yankees can use all the relief pitching help they can get these days. Due to injuries, it seems like they are always improvising to fill the unit with reliable arms, signing or claiming guys such as Justin Topa (already DFA’d), Michael Fulmer, and John Schreiber in the last week or so.

They need some stability in the mid-to-late innings. Fortunately, one of their homegrown guys is getting ready and shaping up as an option at the right time: Clarke Schmidt. At the moment, Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole, Carlos Rodón, Max Fried, Will Warren, and Elmer Rodríguez are ahead of the 2017 first-round pick in the rotation depth chart, with Ryan Weathers potentially rejoining the staff in a few weeks, too. That’s why the organization has already said Schmidt is ticketed for the bullpen when he returns.

To be fair, that’s probably where he’s needed the most. The Yankees’ rotation is better than their bullpen, and they could certainly use an established starter with (successful) relief pitching experience to get through some of the toughest outs in the late innings.

Schmidt, who moved his rehab to Triple-A and pitched two solid innings in which he allowed one run and struck out three on Wednesday, already had a strong season as a bullpen piece back in 2022. That year, he pitched 29 games, starting just three, and posted a 3.12 ERA and a 3.60 FIP in 57.2 innings. He walked 23 and struck out 56.

While it’s true that Schmidt didn’t have a good postseason that year, allowing three runs (and two homers) in three games and 2.1 innings, he is much more mature at this point in his career. After that showing, he has logged three seasons as a starter with mixed but mostly positive results.

A role in relief would allow Schmidt to throw harder in short spurts and maybe focus on some specific pitches, such as the cutter, the knuckle curve, the slider, and the sweeper, with a few four-seamers sprinkled in.

After posting a 26.3 percent strikeout rate in 2024 and a 23.1 mark last year as a starter, Schmidt has some exciting strikeout potential as a reliever, throwing fewer innings at max effort, with the pitching know-how he has gotten over the years. God knows the Yankees need someone who can get some swings and misses in the back of the bullpen.

It’s unclear if manager Aaron Boone will use him as a traditional one-inning reliever or as a multi-inning weapon, but he can thrive in any role. For that to happen, however, he needs to get through his rehab without any setbacks.

Before the two solid frames he racked up on Wednesday for the RailRiders, he had only pitched one game in Double-A, surrendering two runs in 0.2 frames. He is still working his way back from a long layoff following elbow surgery last year, and it stands to reason that he could be rusty whenever he returns to the bigs.

Since Schmidt won’t be starting this year, or at least that’s not the plan at the moment, he is not expected to need too many additional rehab appearances before being ready for activation. In fact, depending on how he feels, there’s a tiny chance his next outing comes in the majors, even though it’s unlikely.

He’ll probably return to starting next year. For now, however, he will help a unit that has the best ERA in the league this season at 3.08, but was 11th with a 3.67 mark in August. As good as the relief corps has been as a whole, the group clearly could use support now, and Schmidt is solid bet to provide it.

items.title: Yankees Birthday of the Day: Eric Plunk
items.author: Jonathan Farrar
items.content:
Trivia nights are a fun activity at local bars, breweries, and restaurants. The best part of trivia is confidently knowing the answer once it is asked. If you ever find yourself faced with the question, “Who is the only Major League Baseball player to be traded for the same Hall of Famer twice in their career?” the answer is former Yankee Eric Plunk. Another trivia tidbit: Plunk is not the reason behind the phrase or term “plunk,” meaning to hit a batter. No, that is simply a fun coincidence, as the term was coined well before Plunk was born or started throwing baseballs.

September 3, 1963 (Wilmington, CA) 1989-1991

Plunk grew up in California and attended Bellflower High School. He was drafted by the Yankees in the 4th round of the 1981 MLB June Amateur Draft. The 6-foot-5 right-handed pitcher had a plus fastball to go along with a good curveball, but scouting reports noted that Plunk would occasionally lose command of his offerings.

The Yankees had Plunk report to the Gulf Coast League after being drafted. Plunk went on to make 11 starts that season, most of them before his 18th birthday. In 1982, Plunk stayed in rookie ball, this time playing in the Appalachian League. After getting his feet wet playing professional ball, Plunk played the 1983 and 1984 seasons for the Yankees farm team in Fort Lauderdale. Over those two seasons at Single-A, Plunk posted a 20-22 record over 48 starts with a 2.81 ERA in 301.1 innings and had established himself as one of the Yankees’ top prospects.

Everything changed for Plunk on December 5, 1984. On that day, he was traded by the New York Yankees with Tim Birtsas, Jay Howell, Stan Javier, and José Rijo to the Oakland Athletics for star leadoff man Rickey Henderson, Bert Bradley, and cash.

Oakland assigned Plunk to their Double-A affiliate to start the 1985 season. Plunk made 13 starts in Double-A, going 8-2 with a 3.52 ERA. That was good enough to get the call-up to Triple-A Tacoma. Plunk would struggle and have to grind out the rest of the season, going 0-5 with a 5.77 ERA.

To start the 1986 season, Plunk was back in Tacoma. After making six starts, Plunk received his first call-up to the major leagues. Plunk made his debut against Toronto on May 12. Plunk stuck on the roster and finished the season with the Athletics, logging 120.1 innings, making 15 starts and appearing in 11 more games as a reliever.

After the season, the Athletics decided they wanted to see what Plunk could be as a reliever. He started the 1987 season back in Tacoma, but was called back up after tossing 34.2 innings with a 1.56 ERA out of the pen, picking up 9 saves in less than a month. Over the rest of the 1987 season in the show, Plunk appeared in 32 games, 11 of which were starts. His final line was 4-6 with a 4.47 ERA and two saves in 95 innings.

Heading into the 1988 season, the Athletics decided to use Plunk as one of the primary set-up men for Hall of Famer Dennis Eckersley. In 1988, Plunk threw 78 innings, all out of the pen, and posted a 3.00 ERA to go along with a 7-2 record. The Athletics made the playoffs after winning the AL West, eventually losing to the Dodgers in the World Series. Plunk worked 2.0 clean innings in the 1988 playoffs.

In 1989, Plunk would make history. After a solid start to the season, on June 21, he was traded from Oakland along with Greg Cadaret and Luis Polonia to the New York Yankees for Rickey Henderson. This was the first and only time to date that a player was traded for the same Hall of Famer twice. The Athletics, with Henderson, would go on to win the World Series in the Battle of the Bay. Plunk, coming full circle back to the team that drafted him, went 7-5 with a 3.69 ERA in pinstripes in 20 relief appearances and 7 starts. The Yankees would finish the season in 5th place in the division.

The Bombers would move Plunk back into his full-time relief role for the 1990 season. Plunk tossed 72.2 innings in 47 games. His ERA was 2.72. The team, however, was not good at all. Posting a record of 67–95, it was the Yankees’ first last-place finish since 1966 and the first last-place in the division era. 95 losses is the most ever by the Yankees, as the 103 losses in 1908 were by the Highlanders.

Plunk was with the Yankees for all of the 1991 season. The team was better, but still not very good. Despite being such a strong reliever, the Yankees decided to use Plunk for spot starts in addition to relieving. Plunk’s ERA went up more than 2 full runs, and he was released by the Yankees following the season.

Prior to the 1992 season, Plunk signed with the Blue Jays but was cut after spring training. He then landed in Cleveland. The Land is where Plunk would spend the next seven seasons. Just like when he arrived in Oakland, Plunk found himself on another team that was on the verge of making a few World Series runs. In another fun piece of trivia Plunk was the first pitcher to win a game at Jacobs Field. Across those seven years in Cleveland, Plunk pitched 462.0 innings, all in relief. His record was 36-33 with a 3.25 ERA, and he picked up 26 saves — though he never pitched particularly well in October (7.53 ERA in 15 games).

In July of 1998, Plunk was traded by Cleveland to the Milwaukee Brewers for Doug Jones. Plunk pitched the rest of 1998 and the 1999 seasons for the Brewers. In 107 innings, he posted a 4.63 ERA and went 5-6. Plunk tried to play the 2000 season but appeared in 7 games for the Cubs’ Double-A affiliate before hanging up his spikes.

Over a 14-year career, Plunk went 72-58 with a 3.82 ERA. In total, at the major league level, he threw 1,151.0 innings and pitched in two World Series. He was hurt for Cleveland’s 1995 loss, but his teams could not pull off the win in either.

After his playing days ended, Plunk remained attached to baseball. Back in California, he started coaching and working privately with players looking to further their development at The Institute of Sports & Education in Corona, CA.

See more of the “Yankees Birthday of the Day” series here.

items.title: Yankees Rivalry Roundup: Mets take two of three from the Rays
items.author: Peter Brody
items.content:
The Mets did their crosstown rivals a huge solid taking two out of three from the Rays, meaning the Yankees closed the gap to 3.5 games with their extra-innings win over the Angels. Cam Schlittler authored another dominant start and Austin Wells supplied the game winner to ensure the team enters the off-day on a positive swell of emotion before heading to San Diego for three.

Here’s how the rest of the games involving the AL playoff picture shook out:

New York Mets (63-77) 10, Tampa Bay Rays (83-56) 4

Neither team’s starting pitching plans went according to script. Griffin Jax was only able to give the Rays 2.2 innings in his first start off the IL, allowing six runs (three earned) on seven hits and two walks. The Mets meanwhile tried to get cute with a bullpen game, only to watch opener Justin Hagenman and reliever Chris Devenski combine to give up four runs on six hits and a walk in 3.2 innings.

New York scored the first six runs of this contest, starting with three in the first. Juan Soto singled and Carson Benge walked to set up a two-run single from Jared Young aided by a missed catch error by the catcher on a play at the plate. Marcus Semien then drove in Young with a double. Two innings later, they scored another three runs. Bo Bichette singled, Semien walked, and A.J. Ewing singled to load the bases with two outs. A Brett Baty double promptly unloaded them to make it 6-0.

Tampa Bay responded with four unanswered, starting with one in the third as Taylor Walls walked, Yandy Díaz singled, and Jonathan Aranda plated Walls with a single. Three more came the following inning, Chandler Simpson and Cedric Mullins reaching on singles to set up a three-run blast to right by Richie Palacios.

Then it was the Mets’ turn to score four unanswered. Three of those arrived in the seventh as Bichette doubled, Benge singled, and Semien was hit by a pitch to load the bases. They received their second bases-clearing double of the night, this one courtesy of rookie Nick Morabito, his first ever big league hit. Soto demolished a solo shot in the eighth to push the Mets into double digits.

Seattle Mariners (66-74) 8, Boston Red Sox (75-65) 3

Bryce Miller was pulled after just 65 pitches despite no report of an injury — a curious decision given he had held the Red Sox to a run in 4.2 innings to that point. It was even more curious considering the Mariners had spotted hima 4-0 lead with a long rally in the third. Weston Wilson and J.P. Crawford hit a pair of leadoff singles and Dominic Canzone walked, Julio Rodríguez and Josh Naylor then following with their own back-to-back singles as Seattle plated four with the help of a wild pitch and a Jarren Duran throwing error.

The lone damage against Miller came in the fourth on a Trevor Story RBI double. However, Seattle responded with another four-run inning in the sixth. Cole Young got plunked, Wilson walked, and Crawford singled to load the bases with no outs. Jhonny Pereda singled home a pair, Randy Arozarena another, and a Canzone double made it 8-1.

Roman Anthony grabbed a consolation run with a solo home run in the seventh and Mickey Gasper and Eli White added another with back-to-back doubles, but that would conclude the scoring. With the loss and Yankees win, the Red Sox fall five games back of second place.

Houston Astros (71-69) 2, Chicago White Sox (73-66) 3

We had a true pitchers’ duel on our hands, Davis Martin giving the White Sox 5.2 scoreless allowing five hits and a walk while Hayden Wesneski was even better for the Astros — seven scoreless innings of one-hit ball with two walks and five strikeouts. Houston had the first real chance to score, with runners on the corners with no outs after Yordan Alvarez led off the fourth with a double and Isaac Paredes followed with a single, but Martin buckled down to strand them in place.

Chicago squandered a golden opportunity in the eighth after Tristan Peters led off with a triple and Drew Romo drew a walk to put runners on the corners with nobody out. However, Peters got thrown out at home on a groundball. Munetaka Murakami singled to load the bases, but Miguel Vargas killed the rally with the inning ending double play.

Houston capitalized in the bottom of the frame, Alvarez singling, Paredes walking, and Jose Altuve getting grazed by a pitch to load the bases with one out. Nelson Velázquez supplied the game winning hit with a two-run single off Sean Newcomb.

Toronto Blue Jays (69-71) 11, Cleveland Guardians (70-69) 0

The Blue Jays bludgeoned Joey Cantillo for nine runs (four earned) in 5.1 innings. Those five unearned runs all came in the second when a throwing error by shortstop Angel Genao allowed two runs to score. The very next batter was Vladimir Guerrero Jr., and he completed the humiliation with a booming three-run blast. Dylan Cease kept pace with Schlittler in the AL Cy Young race, twirling six shutout allowing four hits and no walks with four strikeouts. Vladito would collect another pair of RBIs late and finish with three hits in this rout of the Guardians.

Colorado Rockies (54-86) 6, Baltimore Orioles (69-71) 5

Luis Robert Jr. drove in a pair on his Orioles debut while Trevor Rogers struck out eleven across 6.2 innings of two-run ball. However, the Rockies kept chipping away until a Zac Veen RBI double with two outs in the bottom of the ninth sent the game to extras. In the 11th, Samuel Basallo and Blaze Alexander slapped a pair of RBI singles, but Colorado walked it off by scoring three in the bottom half on TJ Rumfield RBI single, Adael Amador ground-rule double, and the walk-off two-run single by Brett Sullivan.

Athletics (54-86) 9, Texas Rangers (69-71) 2

It was a home run parade for the Athletics in Arlington, four different players leaving the yard. Rookie Nick Bolte became the first player in franchise history to hit two home runs and steal a base from the leadoff spot as he went 3-for-4 with four RBIs. Zack Gelof and Jonah Heim both hit solo shots while Alika Williams provided pop from the bottom of the order with a two-run blast and an RBI double. This was all after Texas jumped out to an early 2-0 lead on solo homers by Ezequiel Duran and Justin Foscue.

items.title: The Yankees’ top defensive plays of August
items.author: Sam Chapman
items.content:
Another month of Yankees baseball is in the books, and though their situation in the American League East has changed little of late, there was plenty of good baseball to take in. With each passing game comes more moments to remember and appreciate, including those made by Yankee defenders. August was no different, as we saw plenty of web gems in the Bronx this month, so let’s take a look back at some of the best from the last month.

August 4: Lombard’s slick play starts a double play

While the defensive slump George Lombard Jr. found himself for part of August is likely the lasting memory, the month also brought plenty of highlight reel plays. Here, early in the month against the Cardinals, the rookie backhanded a sharp two hopper before throwing across his body to kick off an inning-ending double play. Despite the low points of late, we should be seeing highlights at short from Lombard Jr. for years to come.

August 5: The rookie fully extends up the middle

Speaking of which, why not take a look at another gem from Lombard Jr.? Here, just a day after our first featured play, the Yankees shortstop dove to stop a one-hopper destined for center field. Lombard Jr., after fully extending, quickly got up and threw a seed over to first base, just barely nabbing St. Louis’ JJ Wetherholt. The bad sticks out this month, but there was a of good to soak in from Lombard Jr. in August.

August 7: García Jr. fully over the shoulder

Another play from the first week of August, this time with Luis García Jr.’s range on display. With the go-ahead run on third base in the tenth inning for Atlanta, the Yankees first baseman was in a full sprint straight backwards, only to reach over his shoulder and snag the would-be blooper. Not exactly known for his defense, García Jr.’s clutch play saved the game in extras, putting an end to the Braves’ half of the inning. Even sweeter, it was a game the Yankees would eventually win in the bottom half of the inning.

August 18: Austin Wells slides in foul territory

Anyone with experience donning the gear can attest to how difficult a pop up can be from the catching position. Here, Austin Wells makes a difficult one look pretty straightforward. Jackson Holliday lofted a ball toward the third base dugout into foul territory. Immediately set on his intention, Wells ran full speed to the warning track, calling for the ball the entire time, before sliding on a knee to secure the out for his club. Sometimes, making the tough ones look easy can be a highlight on its own.

August 28: Bellinger preserves the lead with his arm

Perhaps more than almost anyone else, Cody Bellinger is a regular on these monthly lists. Toward the end of the month, Belli changed things up, this time making the cut with an exceptional play not with the glove, but with his arm. With the Yankees holding just a 1-0 lead in the seventh, Bellinger caught a relatively shallow fly ball, before perfectly timing his crow hop, and delivering a one-hop strike to home plate. His perfect throw nabbed the runner at home, and preserved what would remain an important 1-0 win for the Yankees at home against the Red Sox.

items.title: Who will join the Yankees’ Circle of Trust?
items.author: Jake Devin
items.content:
Of all the Yankees moves (or non-moves) this summer, their decision not to add pitching at the trade deadline probably caused the most consternation. The team’s pitching staff paced the league in the first half, sure, but most fans looked at the club’s bullpen, and at the long list of names on the IL, and figured the Yankees could use an extra arm or two just in case, just to add a little depth if things got hairy.

Well, we’re here in September, and things have gotten hairy, but the Yankees’ pitching staff has still performed. Max Fried and Ryan Weathers hit the IL with an elbow issues, and Fernando Cruz’s injury left the late-inning crew thin, and yet the Yankees’ team ERA of 2.77 since August 4th leads baseball. Their depth has been tested, and they’ve aced the test.

All that said, outside of David Bednar, Brent Headrick, and Paul Blackburn, there’s no obvious pecking order in the Yankee bullpen. Aaron Boone has three clear favorite options, and then a bunch of question marks. Other than the matter of how to structure the team’s outfield, this might be the most pressing roster concern to sort out in the final month. So, who will emerge as the next most trustworthy reliever in Boone’s bullpen?

I think the most fun part of this question is that the answer could be anyone, thanks to the Yankees’ proclivity for getting the best out of unheralded pitchers. Anyone that is currently on the roster, or working on things in Triple-A, or rehabbing from injury, is liable to step in and surprise us, because Matt Blake and his staff have been so proficient at molding flawed pitchers into serious contributors.

That leaves us with loads of possible players who could emerge in September to establish themselves in the Circle of Trust before the playoffs begin. We could start with the young big leaguers coming back from injuries, Luis Gil, Clarke Schmidt, and Ryan Weathers. Gil, who missed most of this year with a shoulder problem, has returned as a reliever and looked intriguing, sitting 96 mph with his fastball in an outing on Monday night and generating six whiffs. Schmidt is coming off a longer layoff post Tommy John surgery, but also has a high-quality track record; his 3.07 ERA across 2024 and 2025 speaks to how effective he can be when healthy. Weathers morphed into one of the best starters in baseball after a midseason repertoire shift, and could be a dynamite bullpen weapon if he can make it back healthy. It wouldn’t be a surprise to see any of this trio become a key bullpen figure by the end of the month.

Then, there are the late-season scrap heap finds that the Yankees are actively working on. Last week, they dusted off Michael Fulmer, best known around here for swiping the 2016 Rookie of the Year award from Gary Sanchez, and also claimed John Schreiber off waivers. Fulmer has made three appearances with New York and flashed a somewhat interesting cutter-led arsenal, while Schreiber tossed a scoreless inning his Yankees debut Tuesday night and was a dependable middle reliever as recently as last year. It’s entirely possible both with will be off the roster before long, but would you be shocked if one of them benefited from working with Blake and proved they had something left in the tank?

From there, we have the arms in the minors that might seem like long shots, but have performed in the bigs before. The most interesting name is probably Angel Chivilli, who used a sharp changeup to dominate through the month of July before a six-run blowup against the Cardinals in early August ruined his season numbers. The Yankees also have Yerry De los Santos and Brendan Beck as possible options in Scranton. No, no ones wants the Yankees to be relying on these kinds of guys in October, and it’s unlikely any emerge as real options, but it’s not out of the realm of possibility they return to the bigs in September and show something. Elmer Rodríguez could’ve fit with this group of minors options, but he’s back with the big-league squad, and he too merits mention as someone that could earn Boone’s faith with a strong showing this month.

The fact of the matter is, the Yankees have some unsettled spots in the bullpen, and one month to decide who should fill them. Who do you think will step up? Will one or more of these guys find themselves adding to the Circle of Trust?

The Yankees are off today, getting some time to make the short jaunt down from Anaheim to San Diego. There will be plenty on the site to keep you busy, as Sam runs down the Yankees Plays of August, and Peter recaps Wednesday’s American League action. Later, Jonathan profiles Eric Plunk, the only player ever traded for the same Hall of Famer twice, while Andrés discusses Clarke Schmidt’s impending addition to the Yankee bullpen, and the rapid ascent of Yankee prospect Yostin Pena.

items.title: Yankees news: Cole opines on Angels sale
items.author: Kento Mizuno
items.content:
New York Daily News | Gary Phillips: Gerrit Cole grew up an Angels fan, so it’s only natural that he would have something to say about the franchise’s recent sale to Kroenke Sports & Entertainment. However, the veteran approached the issue from a business standpoint rather than an emotional one, noting that the club’s ultimate price tag of $4 billion was remarkably high, especially when compared to the Padres, who were sold for $3.9 billion earlier this year despite being much more competitive in recent years. Said Cole: “It shows that there’s ability to get top dollar on both ends of the spectrum…I think that would speak to how healthy economically the game is functioning.” Definitely something to keep in mind as the MLBPA and the owners continue their standoff. 

NJ.com | Randy Miller: With rosters having expanded on September 1st, the Yankees’ additions were 3B Ryan McMahon and reliever John Schreiber. Here, Miller liaises with an anonymous scout who shares his evaluations on several players who were passed over, including pitching prospect and 2026 debutant Brendan Beck, and former regulars Anthony Volpe and Jasson Dominguez. The scout doesn’t really tell us anything new about the latter two, but his comments on Beck are interesting; he pegs him as a fifth starter and a trade chip of some value despite his relatively advanced age. Not bad for a guy who was drafted 55th overall, then had Tommy John surgery just six months after. 

The Athletic | Asli Petit: In a first for MLB, the Yankees now have an official tampon! Sequel, an upstart company founded by two women ex-athletes, has partnered with the club to offer free tampons in Yankee Stadium’s women’s bathrooms. I wouldn’t have guessed that the Yankees of all teams would be the first team to embark on such a partnership, but it’s a welcome change and an important step towards ensuring the inclusion of female fans. Hopefully more clubs will follow suit!

ESPN.com: The Yankees have struggled to close the gap between them and the Rays in the division race (though it’s certainly closer now than it once was). It’s still a long shot, but the Yankees have one thing going for them; the remaining strength of schedule. The Yankees’ upcoming opponents have a collective winning percentage of .489, markedly lower than the Rays’ slate of .517. The two teams are set to face off in the penultimate series of the season. Here’s hoping the Yankees can handle their business against their lackluster opponents leading up to that all-too-important matchup.

A couple of tweets to round out today’s roundup: first, a quick overview of how Spencer Jones has produced since his second call-up. I have never been more happy to eat crow, and I hope Jones forces me to continue my raven-based diet. 

Second, Clarke Schmidt inches nearer to his return, as he’s been reassigned from Double-A to Triple-A for his rehab. With the Yankees piggybacking Max Fried and Will Warren on Friday, it’s fair to wonder if Schmidt could also be a piggyback candidate should he rejoin the big league club according to schedule.

items.title: Yankees secure series in extras thanks to clutch Wells, dominant Schlittler
items.author: Peter Brody
items.content:
How good has Austin Wells been of late? Initially starting this game on the bench, Wells joined the action in the eighth with a pinch-hit single to prime his bat for the true decisive blow — the go-ahead two-out, two-run single in the tenth to salvage a win from a day when it looked like the offense would squander another brilliant Cam Schlittler start.

Schlittler’s velocity was down about a tick-and-a-half from his amped up last start against the Red Sox, but that didn’t sap any of his effectiveness. After walking a career-high five batters his last time out (albeit across 5.2 scoreless against Boston), there seemed to be a concerted effort to really attack the zone. This led to quick outs on a lot of early contact in the opening innings before he honed his command to the edges, leading to an uptick in strikeouts toward the end of his outing.

He got three straight groundouts in the third and then navigated around a Vaughn Grissom single to leadoff the second by striking out Moisés Ballesteros on a pair of overpowering fastballs. The third and fourth brought another strikeout each, Schlittler remaining economical with his pitch count in both frames. The fifth saw him shift into high gear as he was able to gas a pair of four-seamers by Ballesteros and Christian Moore for his fifth and sixth strikeouts.

Schlittler needed to be shutdown given the way the offense struggled against Reid Detmers. Widely expected to get traded at the deadline, the Angels hung on to their starter and he rewarded them with a 1.55 ERA in eight starts since the break. The bats had no answer the first time through the order, Detmers needing just 30 pitches to make it through three perfect innings.

The script flipped upon facing him for the second time, Paul Goldschmidt and Cody Bellinger opening the fourth with a pair of singles. Heliot Ramos couldn’t follow suit, grounding into what is already his fifth double play in 76 plate appearances for the Yankees. However, Ben Rice kept the inning alive with a two-out infield single, allowing Amed Rosario to open the scoring with an RBI ground-rule double that one-hopped the fence in right. However, you couldn’t help but feel they left meat on the bone between the Ramos GIDP and Spencer Jones striking out to strand Rice at third.

There was a scary moment in the sixth when a Rice foul line drive struck a camera man in the head near the Yankees’ dugout, and it was relieving to see him get up under his own power and get carted off after an over ten minute delay. To Detmers’ credit, he settled down after the fourth, retiring ten of the final 11 batters he faced to end his outing with seven innings of one-run ball.

Schlittler kept cruising through the sixth, punching out Oswald Peraza on a gross curveball and Travis D’Arnaus looking on a painted heater. He got two outs into the seventh to make it 17 retired in a row before making his lone mistake of the outing, and unfortunately for him it left the yard, Grissom crushing a center-cut cutter to dead center just over the outstretched glove of Jones at the wall.

His pitch count was only at 83, so it was a no-brainer to send Schlittler back out for the eighth. He retired the side in order to complete eight innings for the third time this season. It was also his fifth straight start giving up one or fewer runs, and 19th such start overall on the year to set a new franchise record. He had all his pitches working, it’s just a shame the one mistake he made got punished on a night when his offense couldn’t hold up their end of the bargain. He ended his outing having given up a run on two hits and no walks with nine strikeouts in eight innings.

David Bednar was tasked with pitching a scoreless ninth to give his offense a chance in extra innings, and he did so with aplomb, striking out three to nullify a Mike Trout single. Off to extras this game went, the Yankees loading the bases with one out on a José Caballero single and Jazz Chisholm Jr. walk. A Luis García Jr. infield fly put them on the brink of wasting the opportunity, but it also brought one of their most clutch hitters of late to the plate in Wells.

Wells fouled off three straight elevated heaters before getting one he could handle, grounding a single just past the dive attempts of the first and second basemen to plate a pair and take the lead. That opened the floodgates against reliever Luke Murphy, who gave up three straight singles to Bellinger, Trent Grisham, and Rice, each one plating an additional run to make it 6-1 in favor of the Yankees by the time Rosario flew out to end the frame.

Recent bullpen signing Michael Fulmer was entrusted to record the final three outs, and he certainly made us sweat a little. He gave up a two-run blast to Ballesteros, but bounced back to retire the next two batters and nail down the victory, 6-3.

That is what you are supposed to do against the worst team in baseball. Stay in the game long enough until you expose their fatal flaw — in this case, LA’s bullpen — and then capitalize on the opportunities you create for yourself. It’s the Yankees’ fourth series win out of their last five as they become the second team in the AL to reach 80 wins and draw within 3.5 games of the Rays after they lost to the Mets earlier in the day.

The Yankees get tomorrow off before making the short journey to San Diego for three games. Max Fried is scheduled to make his second start back from his latest IL stint facing Walker Buehler in the opener Friday night. First pitch is scheduled for 9:40 p.m. ET with the broadcast remaining on YES.
